strengths: Proposes a unified multimodal flow framework for crystal generation that decouples flow time axes for atom types and crystal structures, enabling CSP, DNG, and atom-type generation within a single model without task-specific retraining.

Reports competitive empirical results: MCFlow-B attains the best single-sample CSP match rate among non-template methods on both MP-20 (63.14%) and MPTS-52 (26.46%), and 20-sample MPTS-52 MR of 41.45% surpasses CrystalFlow (40.37%). DNG results show the best average rank (2.38) among CHGNet-relaxed models, with high metastability (87.3%) and compositional validity (89.85%).

Introduces composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering plus hierarchical inter-/intra-orbit permutation augmentation, with an analysis showing a reduction of the permutation space by over 11 orders of magnitude for N=20, and ablation results indicating that removing these components degrades CSP/DNG performance.

Provides extensive experimental details including three model scales, ablations, sensitivity analysis for noisy guidance, scaling behavior, and additional MPTS-52 results, along with training/inference hyperparameters and compute resources.
weaknesses: The core atom-ordering mechanism is critically underspecified at inference. The ordering relies on Wyckoff positions and space-group information, but in CSP only the composition is known. Algorithm 2 does not explain how atoms are ordered during sampling for CSP or DNG; if target-structure Wyckoff positions are used, the CSP evaluation is invalid, and if arbitrary ordering is used, the model is out-of-distribution relative to its training distribution.

The ordering ablation is confounded. The “– PosEmb” ablation removes all positional information rather than comparing the proposed electronegativity/Wyckoff ordering against a random or alternative ordering with positional embeddings intact, so it does not isolate the benefit of the proposed ordering. No ablation compares different sorting keys (e.g., atomic number vs. electronegativity).

There is an unaddressed train-test mismatch in flow times: training clips t,s to 0.9, but inference trajectories use t=1 and/or s=1 (Algorithm 2). The paper does not explain how the model avoids numerical blow-up at the terminal time, e.g., the discrete rate vector has a 1/(1-t) factor that is undefined at t=1.

Atom-type generation is weakly evaluated. The only baseline is deterministic CGCNN, and MCFlow’s single-sample MR (3.12%) is lower than CGCNN (4.71%); the claimed advantage relies on 20-sample generation, which is not directly comparable to a single deterministic prediction. No generative baseline for structure-conditioned composition generation is provided.

The novelty is incremental: decoupled multimodal flow (Multiflow/Rojas et al.), DiT backbones (ADiT), Wyckoff-based ordering (Wyckoff Transformer), and noisy guidance are adapted from prior work. The paper does not clearly isolate a unique algorithmic contribution beyond combining these components.

The benefit of unification is not quantified. There is no comparison to task-specific models trained with the same architecture, ordering, and data, so it remains unclear whether the unified model improves over or merely matches separately trained models.
Limitations discussion is thin. It mentions scaling to larger cells and property modalities but omits the inference ordering issue, terminal-time mismatch, and failure cases.
Presentation has inconsistencies: notation conflicts (L^l vs. L^t), undefined symbols (‡), duplicate/incorrect references, and several key procedural details only in appendices.

strengths: The paper proposes a unified multimodal flow framework for crystal generation that decouples flow time axes for atom types and structures, enabling CSP, DNG, and atom-type generation within a single model. This is a sensible and potentially useful direction for the crystal generative modeling community.

The technical components for continuous and discrete modalities are mostly standard but appropriate: Riemannian flow on the torus for fractional coordinates, straight-line/geodesic paths for lattice parameters, and CTMC/masked discrete flow for atom types. The appendix provides detailed algorithms, model configurations, and training settings.

The composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering and hierarchical permutation augmentation are intuitively reasonable ways to inject crystallographic priors into a transformer without explicit symmetry templates. The idea of ordering by electronegativity and Wyckoff position, then applying inter- and intra-orbit permutation augmentation, is a plausible soft inductive bias.

On the larger MPTS-52 benchmark, MCFlow shows competitive CSP performance (e.g., MCFlow-L 20-sample MR 41.45 vs CrystalFlow 40.37 and DiffCSP 34.02), and DNG results show reduced mode collapse toward low-symmetry space groups such as P1 compared to FlowMM and ADiT.

The paper includes useful additional analyses in the appendix, including scaling behavior, permutation-space reduction, noisy guidance sensitivity, and template-conditioned comparisons, which improve transparency about the method's behavior.
weaknesses: A critical train-test mismatch undermines the main results: the paper clips flow times t,s <= 0.9 during training (Table 9), but at inference the observed modality is fixed at time 1 (Algorithm 2 for CSP and ATG). The model therefore extrapolates to unseen time embeddings for the conditioning modality, which can invalidate the reported CSP and atom-type generation performance. The paper neither discusses nor ablates this issue.

The atom ordering for CSP is ill-defined. Ordering atoms by Wyckoff position requires structural symmetry information, which is unavailable when only the composition is given. It is unclear how the input atom types are ordered at inference for CSP: if ground-truth Wyckoff positions are used, this is an information leak; if not, the training and inference orderings differ, creating a distribution shift. The paper does not clarify this point, making the CSP setup suspect.

The central ablation does not isolate the proposed ordering. The '-PosEmb' ablation removes positional embeddings entirely, which trivially destroys the model's ability to distinguish atom order, rather than testing the specific electronegativity/Wyckoff ordering against alternatives such as random ordering, electronegativity-only, or Wyckoff-only ordering. Thus the claimed benefit of the proposed ordering is not rigorously supported.

Novelty is incremental. Decoupled multimodal flow with modality-specific time axes is directly adapted from Multiflow and Rojas et al.; ordering by Wyckoff positions follows prior work such as Wyckoff Transformer and Crystalformer; hierarchical permutation augmentation is a natural symmetry augmentation. The 'any-to-any' framing is also overstated, as only two modalities are considered and only three task variants are evaluated.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor. No error bars or multiple random seeds are reported for any benchmark, despite crystal generation metrics being high-variance. DNG comparisons mix models with inconsistent relaxation protocols (e.g., ADiT has an unexplained double-dagger symbol versus the single-dagger CHGNet criterion), and the reported 'Avg Rank' is selective and potentially misleading.

The atom-type generation task uses only a deterministic CGCNN baseline, which is not a generative model. There are no comparisons to generative composition models or simple frequency-based baselines, making the reported gains difficult to interpret.

The CSP main table does not show clear superiority: on MP-20 20-sample generation, MCFlow-B and MCFlow-L underperform DiffCSP and CrystalFlow (77.12/76.08 vs 77.93/78.34). The paper claims competitive performance, but the gains on MP-20 are marginal, and the stronger MPTS-52 results may partly reflect larger model capacity rather than the proposed method.

Reproducibility is limited. No code is released, and key preprocessing details are missing, including the tolerance used for symmetry detection, how orbit decomposition is performed, how disordered/partial-occupancy structures are handled, and the exact MPTS-52 time-slice splits. These details are necessary for others to build on the contribution.

The limitations discussion is minimal and ignores the core methodological concerns above. It only mentions scaling to larger unit cells and does not address the time-clipping mismatch, the CSP ordering ambiguity, the lack of isolated ablations, or the limited any-to-any evaluation.

Presentation and reference quality are poor. Many citations have incorrect years or authors (e.g., Cao et al. 2024/2025, Deng et al. 2019/2023), appendix equations are garbled or duplicated (e.g., Eq. 17), and table footnotes are inconsistent (the double-dagger in Table 2 is unexplained). These issues hinder clarity and reproducibility.

strengths: Introduces MCFlow, a unified multimodal flow framework that decouples time variables for atom types and crystal structures, enabling crystal structure prediction (CSP), de novo generation (DNG), and atom type generation within a single model. This is a novel and useful contribution to crystal generative modeling.

Proposes a composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering and hierarchical inter-/intra-orbit permutation augmentation, providing a soft inductive bias for Diffusion Transformers without explicit symmetry constraints. Ablation studies (Table 4) show that removing inter-orbit, intra-orbit permutations, or positional embeddings consistently degrades CSP and DNG performance, supporting the usefulness of these components.

Demonstrates competitive performance on MP-20 and MPTS-52 across multiple tasks (Tables 1, 2, 3). For DNG, MCFlow-B achieves an average rank of 2.38 across metrics, better than FlowMM (3.75) and ADiT (3.00), and shows improved coverage of crystallographic symmetry distributions compared to baselines that collapse to low-symmetry space groups like P1 (Figure 4).
Provides extensive implementation details, including model configurations, training hyperparameters, inference settings, and algorithms (Algorithms 1–3, Tables 8–10), which supports reproducibility.
Includes a thoughtful limitations discussion and a positive impact statement, acknowledging challenges in scaling to larger unit cells and suggesting future extension to property modalities.
weaknesses: The composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering relies on Wyckoff positions, which are structural properties derived from the crystal structure. However, for CSP and DNG, the structure (and thus Wyckoff positions) is not available at inference time. The paper does not explain how the ordering is determined at inference. If ground-truth Wyckoff positions are used, this would leak test-time structural information and invalidate the CSP results; if they are not used, there is a train-test mismatch because training uses Wyckoff-based ordering. This is a critical gap that undermines the central claim of operating 'without explicit structural templates' and 'without explicitly conditioning space group or Wyckoff positions.'

The atom type generation task is evaluated only against CGCNN, a deterministic property-prediction baseline, which is not a generative model. The lack of comparison to other generative baselines or simple stochastic baselines makes it difficult to assess the significance of the reported diversity and match rate improvements (Table 3).

The ablation studies do not isolate the effect of the lexicographical ordering itself (e.g., comparing against electronegativity-only ordering or random ordering). While the removal of positional embeddings shows that ordering matters, it remains unclear how much the Wyckoff-based secondary sort contributes versus a simpler composition-based order.

Some equations and references contain typos or formatting issues (e.g., Equation 1 and 17 appear garbled in the provided manuscript; the citation 'Hiller et al., 2024' in the text corresponds to a 1986 reference). While minor, these affect clarity.

The DNG results are mixed across metrics. For example, FlowLLM achieves higher stability (14.2% vs. 15.1% for MCFlow-B? Actually MCFlow-B has 15.1% stability, which is higher; but FlowLLM has higher S.U.N. 3.6% vs. 3.3%). The average rank improvement is modest, and the claim of 'competitive performance' is supported but not overwhelming. The paper could benefit from a more thorough error analysis.

strengths: Introduces a unified any-to-any multimodal flow framework for crystals by decoupling atom-type and structure time axes, enabling CSP, DNG, and structure-conditioned atom-type generation with a single model. This is a novel and useful extension of multimodal flow matching to periodic crystals.

The composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering with hierarchical inter-/intra-orbit permutation augmentation is a sensible soft inductive bias for DiT-based crystal generation. Ablations (Tables 5, H.4, H.8) show that electronegativity ordering, hierarchical augmentation, and decoupled time axes each improve results, and Figure 4 shows better matching of space-group/Wyckoff distributions than FlowMM/ADiT.

The empirical study is broad: MP-20 and MPTS-52, three tasks, three model scales, standardized LeMat-GenBench DNG evaluation with an MLIP ensemble, multiple baselines, additional METRe/filtered-MR/computational-cost analyses, and scaling curves.

Results are competitive in several settings: MCFlow leads on MPTS-52 CSP and on several DNG stability/metastability/RMSD metrics, and the paper establishes structure-conditioned atom-type generation and atom-type substitution as new tasks for a single trained model.

The paper provides training/inference algorithms, model/training/inference configurations, computational cost measurements, and an explicit limitations section, which aids reproducibility and transparently notes the stability-novelty trade-off and inapplicability to amorphous/disordered systems.
weaknesses: The inference-time atom ordering is not specified. The method's ordering is defined using Wyckoff positions, which are available during training but not for CSP or DNG inference. The manuscript does not explain how the input sequence is ordered at test time. If ground-truth Wyckoff positions are used, it is a form of test-time leakage; if not, there is a train/test distribution mismatch. This is central to the claimed template-free symmetry-aware generation.

There is a training/inference time mismatch: flow times t and s are clipped to <= 0.9 during training, but the inference algorithms evaluate the model at t=1 or s=1 for conditioning. This out-of-distribution conditioning is not justified, ablated, or discussed, and could substantially affect the reported CSP/ATG results.

The template-conditioned comparison in Table H.3 is not a fair evaluation. For MCFlow, MR/RMSE are computed only on generated samples that match the target template, i.e., after post-hoc selection using ground-truth template information. This circular protocol cannot support the claim that MCFlow outperforms template-conditioned baselines such as DiffCSP++ and SGFM.

The ablation isolating the proposed ordering is confounded: removing positional embeddings (-PosEmb) removes all sequence-position information, not just the proposed ordering, so the drop cannot be attributed specifically to the ordering. The cumulative ablation labels are also ambiguous.

Performance claims are somewhat overstated. On MP-20 CSP, MCFlow is not consistently better than task-specific baselines (e.g., MCFlow-L single-sample 64.08 vs OMatG 63.75; MCFlow-L multi-sample 76.08 vs DiffCSP 77.93 and CrystalFlow 78.34). In DNG, larger MCFlow variants sacrifice novelty sharply (18.6-19.4% vs 70.5% for MatterGen and 66.2% for DiffCSP), so 'competitive or superior across most metrics' is too broad. ATG baselines are weak (adapted CGCNN/FlowMM) and the atom-substitution result is qualitative only.

Presentation and reproducibility issues remain: many citation years are inconsistent (e.g., Butler et al. 2018 listed as 2025; Glass et al. 2006 as 2024; Jain et al. 2013 as 2024), names are inconsistent (PLaID++/PlaID++, Martiossyan/Mart Grossyan), and several implementation details are missing (inference ordering, CTMC/ODE step implementations, logit-level noisy guidance for ATG, code release).

strengths: Introduces a unified multimodal flow formulation for crystals with decoupled time axes, extending any-to-any multimodal flow matching to periodic crystal systems in a plausible way.
Reports competitive or best results on MPTS-52 crystal structure prediction, with scaling behavior across model sizes and strong stability-related metrics in de novo generation.
Proposes a composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering with hierarchical inter-/intra-orbit permutation augmentation; ablations suggest these components contribute to performance.
Defines and evaluates a structure-conditioned atom type generation task, plus a qualitative atom substitution study, broadening the set of crystal generation tasks considered.
Discusses limitations and broader impacts, including the stability-novelty trade-off and inapplicability to amorphous/disordered systems.
weaknesses: Critical inference-time atom ordering is not specified. The proposed ordering relies on Wyckoff positions/space group, but CSP provides only composition and DNG provides no structure at all. The paper does not explain how to define the ordered sequence at inference. If ground-truth Wyckoff positions are used, this leaks target structural information into CSP; if they are not used, the model is evaluated under a different ordering than during training. This undermines the central CSP/DNG claims and reproducibility.

There is a train/inference mismatch in flow time conditioning. Training clips flow times t and s to 0.9, yet CSP and ATG inference query the model at t=1 or s=1 (e.g., Algorithm 3). No ablation or justification is provided for this extrapolation, so the conditional generation mechanism is not rigorously supported.

DNG evaluation with pre-relaxation is potentially biased: MCFlow uses Orb-v3 for pre-relaxation, while Orb-v3 is also one of the three MLIPs in the evaluation ensemble. This likely improves MCFlow's stability and E_hull metrics relative to baselines, and the baselines' pre-relaxation protocols are not controlled.

DNG novelty is substantially lower than strong baselines (e.g., MCFlow-L reports 18.6/19.4% novelty versus 66.2% for DiffCSP and 70.5% for MatterGen). The paper acknowledges a stability-novelty trade-off but still claims competitive or superior performance across most metrics; novelty is a key discovery metric, so this trade-off limits significance.

The ordering ablation is insufficient. Removing PosEmb eliminates all positional information rather than isolating the proposed ordering, and Table H.4 does not separate the effect of Wyckoff sorting from electronegativity sorting. The claim that the ordering injects crystallographic symmetry is therefore not cleanly supported.

The ATG evaluation is weak: only adapted CGCNN and FlowMM are compared, multi-sample FlowMM results are missing, and no strong structure-conditioned generative baseline is included. The atom-substitution evidence is qualitative, often recovers the original masked element, and claimed space-group matches are not verified in the table.

Mathematical and presentation errors reduce confidence. Appendix A.3 contains an incorrect conditional velocity expression (u(x_t,t|x0,x1)=log_{x_t}(x0)/π(x0,x1)) and a duplicated equation; many reference years are wrong (e.g., Butler 2025 vs 2018, Jain 2024 vs 2013), suggesting sloppy preparation. No code or data availability statement is provided.

The 'any-to-any' claim is only partially demonstrated. Only two modalities and three inference trajectories are explored; partial-modality or joint conditional generation is not systematically evaluated. The claim of avoiding explicit structural templates is also misleading because Wyckoff positions are derived from crystallographic symmetry/templates.

strengths: Introduces a unified multimodal flow framework for crystals that decouples atom-type and structure time axes, enabling a single model to support CSP, DNG, structure-conditioned atom type generation, and atom type substitution without task-specific retraining.

The composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering with hierarchical inter-/intra-orbit permutation augmentation is a novel and useful soft inductive bias for transformer-based crystal generation; ablations show clear gains over atomic-number ordering and random permutation.

Extensive empirical evaluation across MP-20, MPTS-52, and LeMat-GenBench, with three model scales, multiple tasks, and numerous baselines. MCFlow achieves best results on MPTS-52 CSP and strong stability/metastability in DNG.

Thorough additional analyses, including noisy guidance ablation, decoupled vs. coupled time-axis ablation, unified vs. CSP-only training, template-conditioned CSP comparison, computational cost, and scaling behavior, support the main claims.
Honest limitations discussion acknowledges inapplicability to amorphous/disordered systems and the stability-novelty trade-off across model scales; the impact statement is appropriate.
The paper tackles a meaningful problem—unifying crystal generation tasks—and demonstrates practical value through atom type substitution with chemically meaningful predictions.
weaknesses: Critical ambiguity in the atom ordering at inference for CSP: the proposed ordering relies on Wyckoff positions, which require space-group and structural information unavailable from composition alone. The paper does not explain how the ordering is defined for CSP (or DNG) without ground-truth structural symmetry. If target Wyckoff positions are used at inference, this constitutes leakage and undermines the claim of template-free CSP; if an arbitrary ordering is used, it may mismatch training and weaken reproducibility and the reported CSP comparisons.

The ablation does not isolate the contribution of Wyckoff-position sorting from electronegativity ordering. The “Electronegativity” row in Table H.4 corresponds to the full model, so the specific benefit of the Wyckoff component is not demonstrated.

Dataset split ambiguity for MPTS-52: the paper states both datasets use a 60/20/20 split but also mentions chronological time slices. If MPTS-52 was randomly split rather than using the standard time-based benchmark split, comparisons with baselines in Table 1 may be invalid.

Results are not uniformly best: on MP-20 multi-sample CSP, MCFlow-L (MR 76.08) trails CrystalFlow (78.34) and DiffCSP (77.93); on DNG novelty, MCFlow-L (18.6/19.4) is far below DiffCSP (66.2/62.0), with a stability-novelty trade-off. The “competitive” claim is fair but should be contextualized more explicitly.

ATG evaluation is limited: baselines are an adapted property predictor (CGCNN) and a DNG model (FlowMM), with no dedicated structure-conditioned composition generation baselines. MCFlow-B single-sample MR (3.12) is lower than CGCNN (4.71) on MP-20, despite higher compositional validity.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: Table 2 uses “ET(eV)” and “Etalk (eV)” for formation energy and energy above hull; reference year inconsistencies exist (e.g., Butler et al. 2018 cited as 2025, multiple 2026 citations), and some equations/notation are difficult to parse.

The theoretical justification for the joint multimodal flow with mixed CTMC/ODE dynamics is brief. While it cites relevant work, the paper could better justify the independent coupling, posterior expectation, and the validity of the weighted divergence objective in the joint time plane.
